paras: The lynching of George Hughes took place in northwest Kemper County, Mississippi, in April 1882, when a crowd took Hughes, a Black tenant farmer, from a constable and hanged him. Hughes had just been committed to jail by a justice of the peace on an accusation that he had raped and murdered Callie Henson, the young wife of the farmer on whose land he lived. Mississippi papers reported the accusation as proved, and several openly approved of the lynching.

According to residents quoted by the Jackson Clarion, Aleck Henson had married 17-year-old Callie Echols, daughter of a Neshoba County farmer, the previous December and settled on a farm in Kemper County near the Neshoba line. Hughes lived with his family in a cabin a few hundred yards from the Henson house. When Henson came home late from plowing and could not find his wife, Hughes joined the search and told him to look in the well, where her body was found.

The Clarion's informants described marks of strangling and a bitten ear, and an inquest before Justice of the Peace Isaac Dawes on Friday morning found that she had died by violence. Suspicion fell on Hughes because of his hint about the well, his presence on the place after Henson left, and the report that his clothes had been changed and washed.

Dawes then examined Hughes in a hearing that lasted until late Friday evening and ordered him committed to the jail at DeKalb. A correspondent of the Newton Free Press wrote that hundreds of people had gathered at the scene and that, once the committing court had finished, "men could not be restrained." Constable William Smith set out with the prisoner for DeKalb, but about half a mile from the hearing a crowd of about 75 took Hughes from him and hanged him at once, according to the Clarion. The Free Press account says he was taken to a tree and hanged there.

No report of an inquest into Hughes's death, of arrests, or of grand jury action appears in the coverage. The Meridian Mercury wrote that the mob had "saved the officers of the law any further trouble about disposing of him."

The story spread through Mississippi papers from two Meridian sources and from informants near the scene. The Jackson Comet printed the first short notice on April 15, saying the accused "was hung by a mob." A summary from the Meridian Observer ran in the Clarion and the Pascagoula Democrat-Star and, outside the state, in the Memphis Daily Appeal; the version in the Clarion and the Appeal ended, "Hanging was too good for him."

The Clarion's longer account, headed "The Kemper Horror" with the subhead "The Brute Lynched," was the only one to name the officers and give a crowd size. The Meridian Mercury, reprinted by the Grenada Sentinel as "Kemper to the Front Again," called the accused a "black demon," praised "the way of the Kemper boys," and taunted "stalwart scoundrels" to "howl long, and loud." The Magnolia Gazette reprinted the Mercury text without credit, and the Brookhaven Ledger headlined its item "Met His Reward." By May the case had shrunk to a single line in the Liberty Southern Herald.

The accounts disagree on dates: the Clarion and the Mercury put the crime on a Thursday and the hearing on the next day, the Observer has the body found on a Saturday, and the Comet dates the crime Friday, April 7. The family name appears as both Henson and Hinson, and the husband as Aleck, Alex., or Heck.

bases: A crowd took George Hughes, a Black tenant committed to jail on an accusation of murder, from a constable and hanged him (A4, A5, A7).

A crowd of about 75 took Hughes from Constable William Smith after a justice committed him to jail and hanged him (A4); the papers present it as punishment for the alleged rape and murder of Mrs. Henson (A5, A8).

The Clarion's local account (A4), the Newton Free Press correspondent (A5), the Meridian Observer (A7) and the Meridian Mercury (A8) independently agree that the accused was taken from the officers after his commitment and hanged.
